parts.prompt: Calculate the value of the machine after $5$ years, giving your answer correct to the nearest dollar.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the overall percentage decrease in the value of the machine over the $5$ years, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: After $k$ complete years, the value of the machine is less than $\$20\,000$ for the first time. Work out the value of $k$.

intro_text: The population, $P$, of an island $t$ years after $1$ January $2020$ is modelled by the formula \\[0.15cm] \hspace*{0.8cm} $P = 12\,500 \times 1.032^t$

parts.label: (b)

parts.label: (c)

parts.prompt: Find the first year in which the population on $1$ January exceeds $18\,000$.

intro_text: On 1 January 2022, Elena bought a new car for $\$24\,500$. The value of the car decreases exponentially by $14\%$ each year.

parts.label: (a)

parts.prompt: The value of the car, $\$V$, $t$ years after 1 January 2022 is modelled by the formula $V = A \times k^{t}$. Write down the value of $A$ and the value of $k$.

parts.label: (c)

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the value of the car on 1 January 2024.\nGive your answer correct to the nearest dollar.

parts.label: (d)

intro_text: A scientist measures the mass, $M$ grams, of a radioactive substance at time $t$ hours after the start of an experiment. The results are shown in the table.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Show that the mass of the substance decays exponentially by $15\%$ each hour.
markscheme: Checks ratios of consecutive masses: $\dfrac{408}{480} = 0.85$, $\dfrac{346.8}{408} = 0.85$, and $\dfrac{294.78}{346.8} = 0.85$ [M1]
States constant multiplier $0.85 = 1 - 0.15$, confirming a $15\%$ exponential decay per hour [A1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of the substance when $t = 8$. Give your answer correct to $1$ decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage decrease in the mass of the substance from $t = 2$ to $t = 6$. Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.
markscheme: Multiplier over $4$ hours $= 0.85^4$ ($= 0.522006...$) or mass at $t = 6$ is $480 \times 0.85^6 = 181.031...$ seen [M1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find the first whole number of hours, $t$, at which the mass of the substance is less than $50$ grams.

intro_text: On $1$ January $2020$, a company purchases an industrial printer for $\$40\,000$ and invests $\$16\,000$ in an equity fund.\n- The value of the printer depreciates exponentially at a rate of $r\%$ each year.\n- The value of the equity fund increases exponentially at a rate of $6.5\%$ each year.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: On $1$ January $2022$, the value of the printer is $\$28\,900$. Find the value of $r$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the value of $t$, in years after $1$ January $2020$, when the value of the equity fund is equal to the value of the printer. Give your answer correct to $2$ decimal places.
markscheme: $\left(\dfrac{1.065}{0.85}\right)^t = 2.5$ or intersection of $y = 16\,000(1.065)^x$ and $y = 40\,000(0.85)^x$ on graph [M1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the integer number of complete years after $1$ January $2020$ until the value of the equity fund is first more than double the value of the printer.
markscheme: $t > 7.137\ldots$ or trials showing $t = 7$ fails ($24\,864 < 25\,646$) and $t = 8$ succeeds ($26\,480 > 21\,799$) [M1]

subparts.prompt: Calculate the value of $E$ when $m = 0.45$, $v = 12.4$, $k = 8.5$, $x = 1.6$ and $t = 2.25$. \\[0.15cm] Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.

parts.label: (a)

intro_text: The time, $t$ minutes, taken by $80$ candidates to complete a practical assessment is recorded. All candidates passed the assessment, and those who completed it in $30$ minutes or less were awarded a Distinction. The incomplete grouped frequency table shows the distribution of times.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write down an equation connecting $p$ and $q$.

parts.label: (b)

subparts.label: (i)

intro_text: A researcher records the time, $t$ minutes, taken by $200$ commuters to travel to work. The data is classified into four continuous class intervals of unequal width, as shown in the table below, where $p$, $q$, and $r$ are positive integers.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the researcher uses class intervals with strict inequality on the left and non-strict inequality on the right (such as $10 < t \le 25$) when tabulating this data.
markscheme: Because time is continuous data, so there must be no gaps between intervals [B1]
So that boundary values belong to a single unique interval without overlapping [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The frequency density of the class $10 < t \le 25$ is $4.2$. The frequency density of the class $25 < t \le 45$ is twice the frequency density of the class $45 < t \le 75$. Calculate the values of $p$, $q$, and $r$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Using your values of $p$, $q$, and $r$, calculate an estimate for the percentage of the $200$ commuters who took more than $35$ minutes to travel to work.

intro_text: A botanist measures the heights, $h$ centimetres, of $120$ seedlings grown under two different light conditions, Condition $X$ and Condition $Y$. The grouped frequency table classifies the heights of the seedlings.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Use the information in the table to answer the following.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Explain why inequality notation such as $10 \le h < 15$ is used to classify the heights rather than $10 - 14$ and $15 - 19$.
markscheme: Height is continuous data, so inequality notation prevents gaps between intervals (e.g. for values between $14$ cm and $15$ cm) and avoids overlapping boundaries [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Show that $a + b = 35$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The total number of seedlings grown under Condition $X$ is $16$ more than the total number of seedlings grown under Condition $Y$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The botanist reclassifies all $120$ seedlings into a two-way table by light condition and whether each seedling is Short ($h < 20$ cm) or Tall ($h \ge 20$ cm). Complete the two-way table.
markscheme: Total row: Condition $X = 68$, Condition $Y = 52$, Grand Total $= 120$ [B2] (or at least two totals correct [B1])

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The botanist later discovers that $5$ seedlings grown under Condition $X$ with heights in the interval $15 \le h < 20$ were misclassified and actually had heights in the interval $20 \le h < 25$. Calculate the percentage of all seedlings grown under Condition $X$ that are now classified as Tall ($h \ge 20$ cm), giving your answer correct to $1$ decimal place.
markscheme: New number of Tall seedlings under Condition $X = 35 + 5 = 40$ [B1]

intro_text: An environmental scientist measures the mass, $m$ grams, of $80$ pebbles collected from a beach. The grouped frequency table shows the distribution of the masses, where $x$ and $y$ are positive integers.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State whether the mass of a pebble is discrete or continuous data.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Show that $5x + y = 60$.
markscheme: $5x + y + 20 = 80$ simplifying to $5x + y = 60$ with no errors seen [A1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: An estimate for the mean mass of the $80$ pebbles, calculated using the midpoints of the intervals, is $46$ g.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Show that $3x + y = 42$.
markscheme: $210x + 70y = 2940$ dividing by $70$ to give $3x + y = 42$ with no errors seen [A1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Solve these simultaneous equations to work out the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.
markscheme: Correct elimination or substitution, such as $(5x + y) - (3x + y) = 60 - 42$ or $2x = 18$ [M1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The scientist decides to regroup the data into two class intervals: $0 < m \le 50$ and $50 < m \le 100$. Write down the minimum and maximum possible number of pebbles in the interval $0 < m \le 50$, and explain why the exact number cannot be determined from the table.
markscheme: The data is grouped, so the exact masses of the $25$ pebbles in $40 < m \le 60$ are unknown [B1]

intro_text: A technology company surveys all $200$ of its employees about their department (Engineering, Design, Marketing) and their primary operating system (Windows, macOS, Linux). \\[0.15cm] The two-way table shows the number of employees in each category, in terms of $x$ and $y$.

Divides throughout by $2$ with no errors to obtain $5x + y = 85$ [A1]

parts.label: (b)

If Company Y has more than $150$ workers, more workers travel by Car at Company Y [B1]

markscheme: Borrowing a book does not mean it was read (or students may read books not borrowed from the school library) [B1]

intro_text: The dual bar chart shows the number of tickets sold by Cinema A and Cinema B on each of four days.

intro_text: Two athletes, Priya and Elena, each run $10$ training races of $100$ metres. The table shows summary statistics for their times, in seconds.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Compare the race times of Priya and Elena. Make two comments, one comparing an average and one comparing the spread.
markscheme: Elena is faster on average because her median time ($12.1$ s) is lower than Priya's ($12.4$ s) [B1]
Priya's times are more consistent (less spread out) because her interquartile range ($0.3$ s) is smaller than Elena's ($0.8$ s) [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Write down the percentage of Elena's races that took $12.1$ seconds or less.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A coach selects one athlete to represent the club in a competition. Give one reason why the coach might choose Priya, and give one reason why the coach might choose Elena.
markscheme: Priya: She is more reliable and less likely to run a very slow race (smaller IQR) [B1]
Elena: She has a faster typical time and is capable of faster times (lower median) [B1]

intro_text: Do not use a calculator in this question. The dual bar chart shows the number of goals scored by two football teams, Rovers and United, in each of four matches.

parts.label: (c)

intro_text: The dual bar chart shows the number of Gold, Silver, and Bronze medals won by Country A and Country B at an international athletics championship.

parts.label: (a)

markscheme: The bar chart only gives the number of medals won and provides no information about the population size of either country [B1]
Winning more medals could be due to other factors such as entering more athletes or better training facilities [B1]

intro_text: Do not use a calculator in this question.\\[0.15cm]The bar chart shows the number of goals scored per match by Team X and Team Y in $20$ matches each.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write down the modal number of goals scored by Team X.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the median number of goals scored by Team Y.
markscheme: Median lies between the $10$th and $11$th match when ordered ($5$ matches with $0$ goals, $8$ matches with $1$ goal) [M1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Work out how many more goals Team X scored in total than Team Y.
markscheme: Team X total $= (0 \times 3) + (1 \times 6) + (2 \times 7) + (3 \times 3) + (4 \times 1) = 33$ and Team Y total $= (0 \times 5) + (1 \times 8) + (2 \times 4) + (3 \times 2) + (4 \times 1) = 26$ [M1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A supporter says: "Team X is more consistent in the number of goals scored per match than Team Y because Team X scored more goals."\\[0.15cm]Explain whether the range supports the supporter's claim about consistency.
markscheme: No, both teams have the same range of $4$ goals ($4 - 0 = 4$), so the spread of goals scored is the same [B1]

intro_text: The dual bar chart shows the number of books borrowed from a school library by Grade $9$ and Grade $10$ students across four genres during one month.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write down the modal genre of books borrowed by Grade $10$ students.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate how many more books were borrowed in total by Grade $10$ students than by Grade $9$ students.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A student makes the following statement:\n"On average, each Grade $10$ student borrowed more books than each Grade $9$ student."\nExplain why this conclusion cannot be justified from the bar chart alone.
markscheme: The bar chart does not show the total number of students in Grade $9$ or Grade $10$ [B1]
If there are more students in Grade $10$ than in Grade $9$, the mean number of books per student could be lower or the same [B1]

intro_text: The dual bar chart shows the number of tickets sold for two films, Film A and Film B, at a cinema over four days.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write down the day on which the difference between the number of tickets sold for Film A and Film B was greatest, and state this difference.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the total number of tickets sold for Film A over the four days.
markscheme: Reads all four values for Film A and adds: $18 + 34 + 48 + 30$ [M1]

parts.prompt: Compare the ticket sales for Film A and Film B over the four days, making two distinct statistical statements.
markscheme: States that Film A sold more tickets than Film B on every day (or had a higher total/mean of $130$ compared to $100$) [B1]
States that both films followed the same daily pattern, peaking on Saturday and having their lowest sales on Thursday (or Film A had a greater range of $30$ compared to $26$ for Film B) [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A cinema manager claims that Film A will also sell more tickets than Film B on Monday. \\[0.15cm] Give one reason why this conclusion may not be valid.
markscheme: The data only covers Thursday to Sunday, so predicting Monday extrapolates beyond the observed days (or Monday is a weekday with different audience patterns) [B1]

parts.prompt: Write down the modal method of travel for both Grade $9$ and Grade $10$.

parts.label: (b)

A second distinct valid comparison supported by values from the chart [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A student looks at the chart and concludes: "Across the entire school, twice as many Grade $10$ students cycle to school as Grade $9$ students." Explain why this conclusion may not be valid.
markscheme: The data comes from a sample of $80$ students from each grade rather than the entire school population [B1]
The total number of students in Grade $9$ and Grade $10$ across the whole school may be different (or the sample may not be representative) [B1]

intro_text: The grouped frequency table shows the weekly overtime, $t$ hours, worked by $50$ employees at the North Branch of a company during one week.

parts.context: For the North Branch,

subparts.prompt: Write down the class interval that contains the median score for Group B.

intro_text: Two groups of students, Group P and Group Q, took the same mathematics test marked out of $100$. \\[0.15cm] The table shows summary statistics for the scores of each group.

parts.prompt: Give one statistical reason why Group P could be considered to have performed better on average, and one statistical reason why Group Q could be considered to have performed better on average.

Group Q has a higher mean ($68.5 > 64.2$) [B1]

parts.prompt: Compare the spread of the scores in Group P and Group Q, supporting your answer with values from the table.

CityLine has more consistent arrival delays than MetroBus because its interquartile range (or range) is smaller ($1.8 < 3.2$) [B1]

parts.label: (b)

parts.prompt: The sample for MetroBus consisted of $12$ buses measured only during morning rush hour, whereas the sample for CityLine consisted of $40$ buses measured throughout the entire day. Give one reason why comparing these two samples may not be fair.
markscheme: The samples were taken at different times of day (rush hour traffic increases delays for MetroBus) or the sample sizes are very different [B1]

intro_text: The table summarises the midday temperatures, in $^\circ$C, recorded during July in two cities, City A and City B.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The lower quartile midday temperature in City A was $22.8^\circ$C. Write down the upper quartile midday temperature in City A.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the midday temperatures in City A and City B. Give two comparisons in context, one comparing the average temperature and one comparing the spread of the temperatures.
markscheme: On average, City A was warmer at midday than City B because its median is higher ($24.5^\circ$C $> 21.0^\circ$C) [B1]
City A had more consistent (less varied) midday temperatures than City B because its IQR ($3.2^\circ$C $< 6.8^\circ$C) and range ($8.0^\circ$C $< 14.5^\circ$C) are smaller [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A tourist looks at the table and states that it did not rain at all in City A during July. Explain why this conclusion cannot be made from the given data.
markscheme: The table only gives data on midday temperatures and provides no information about rainfall [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Another tourist states that every day in July was warmer at midday in City A than in City B. Explain why this statement may not be true.
markscheme: The table only shows summary statistics rather than individual daily temperatures [B1]
With a range of $8.0^\circ$C in City A and $14.5^\circ$C in City B, the coolest days in City A could have been cooler than the warmest days in City B [B1]

intro_text: The table shows summary statistics for the $100$\,m sprint times, in seconds, of two athletes, Maya and Chloe.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Compare the average sprint times of Maya and Chloe using both the mean and the median.
markscheme: Chloe has a faster (lower) mean time ($12.2\text{ s} < 12.4\text{ s}$) [B1]
Maya has a faster (lower) median time ($12.3\text{ s} < 12.5\text{ s}$) [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain which athlete has the more consistent sprint times, giving a statistical reason from the table.
markscheme: Her interquartile range ($0.3\text{ s} < 0.5\text{ s}$) and range ($0.9\text{ s} < 1.4\text{ s}$) are smaller [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Chloe's statistics were calculated from $12$ races. Calculate the total time for all $12$ of Chloe's races.

intro_text: Two schools, North High and South High, carried out a survey on how students travel to school. The table shows the percentage of surveyed students using each method of transport and the total number of students surveyed at each school.

parts.label: (a)

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A student looks at the table and states: "More students walk to school at North High than at South High because $40\%$ is greater than $25\%$." Explain why the student is incorrect.
markscheme: The total numbers of students surveyed are different for the two schools [B1]
North High has $0.40 \times 400 = 160$ students who walk, whereas South High has $0.25 \times 900 = 225$ students who walk [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: At South High, there are $1500$ students in total, so only $900$ students were surveyed. State two conditions required for the percentages in the table to accurately represent all $1500$ students at South High.
markscheme: The sample of $900$ students must be selected at random (unbiased) [B1]
The sample must be representative of the whole school (for example, proportional across all year groups) [B1]

intro_text: The box-and-whisker plots show information about the battery lives, in hours, of samples of smartphones from Brand A and Brand B.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the median and the interquartile range for Brand A.
markscheme: Upper quartile $= 27$ and lower quartile $= 18$ seen [M1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the battery lives of Brand A and Brand B. Make two comparative statements, referring to both average and spread.
markscheme: Brand B has a higher median battery life ($25$ hours compared to $23$ hours), so Brand B lasts longer on average [B1]
Brand A has a smaller interquartile range ($9$ hours compared to $16$ hours) [or smaller range: $24$ hours vs $28$ hours], so Brand A's battery life is more consistent [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A sample of $60$ smartphones of Brand B was tested. \\[0.15cm] Estimate how many of these smartphones had a battery life between $15$ hours and $25$ hours.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A customer claims: "At least $10$ smartphones in the Brand B sample had a battery life of exactly $25$ hours." \\[0.15cm] Explain why this claim cannot be confirmed from the box-and-whisker plot.
markscheme: A box-and-whisker plot only shows quartiles and extreme values, not individual data values or their frequencies [B1]

intro_text: The box-and-whisker plots show information about the daily journey times, in minutes, of $60$ commuters using Route $A$ and $60$ commuters using Route $B$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: For Route $A$, find

subparts.label: (ii)

parts.label: (b)

markscheme: Calculates Route $B$ median $= 28$ minutes and Route $B$ interquartile range $= 46 - 22 = 24$ minutes [B1]
On average, Route $B$ is faster because its median ($28$ minutes) is lower than Route $A$'s median ($32$ minutes) [B1]
Route $A$ has more consistent journey times because its interquartile range ($16$ minutes) is smaller than Route $B$'s interquartile range ($24$ minutes) [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Estimate the number of commuters on Route $B$ whose journey time was more than $46$ minutes.

intro_text: The box-and-whisker plots show the distributions of battery life, in hours, for samples of two brands of smartphone, Brand X and Brand Y.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Find the interquartile range of the battery life for

subparts.label: (i)

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Brand Y.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of battery life for Brand X and Brand Y, referring to both average and spread.
markscheme: Brand Y has a higher median ($21\text{ hours} > 20\text{ hours}$), so Brand Y lasts longer on average [B1]

Brand X has a smaller interquartile range ($7\text{ hours} < 8\text{ hours}$), so the middle $50\%$ of Brand X battery lives are slightly more consistent (or Brand Y has a smaller range, $15\text{ hours} < 16\text{ hours}$) [B1]

parts.label: (c)

markscheme: Cites specific overlapping values, e.g. the minimum of Brand Y is $14$ hours whereas the maximum of Brand X is $28$ hours (or median $20$ hours) [B1]
Explains that some Brand Y phones therefore have a shorter battery life than at least half of the Brand X phones [B1]

intro_text: The cumulative frequency graphs show the distribution of battery life, in hours, for $80$ batteries of Brand X and $80$ batteries of Brand Y.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Use the cumulative frequency graphs to find the median and the interquartile range for

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Brand X,

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Brand Y.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the battery lives of Brand X and Brand Y, making two distinct statistical statements.
markscheme: Brand Y lasts longer on average because its median ($32$ hours) is greater than Brand X's ($25$ hours) [B1]
Brand Y's battery life is more consistent because its interquartile range ($7$ hours) is smaller than Brand X's ($10$ hours) [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A technician needs a battery that lasts for more than $35$ hours. Determine which brand has more batteries meeting this requirement, showing your working clearly.
markscheme: Brand X: $80 - 72 = 8$ batteries and Brand Y: $80 - 60 = 20$ batteries [M1]

intro_text: Two groups of workers, Group P and Group Q, each assemble an identical electronic component. The box-and-whisker plots show the distribution of the times taken, in minutes, by the workers in each group.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the median and the interquartile range for Group P.

parts.label: (b)

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Compare the assembly times of Group P and Group Q, making two distinct statistical statements in context.
markscheme: On average, Group P assembled the component faster than Group Q because Group P's median time is lower ($25\text{ min} < 30\text{ min}$) [B1]
Group P's assembly times were more consistent than Group Q's because Group P's interquartile range ($10\text{ min} < 15\text{ min}$) and range ($28\text{ min} < 32\text{ min}$) are smaller [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: There are $60$ workers in Group P and $48$ workers in Group Q. Estimate the total number of workers across both groups who took more than $30$ minutes to assemble the component.
markscheme: Group P ($30$ min is upper quartile): $0.25 \times 60 = 15$ [M1]

intro_text: Two archers, Elena and Marcus, each shoot $12$ arrows at a target. Elena's scores are recorded below. \\[0.15cm] \begin{center} $7$ \quad $9$ \quad $6$ \quad $10$ \quad $8$ \quad $9$ \\[0.15cm] $5$ \quad $8$ \quad $10$ \quad $7$ \quad $9$ \quad $8$ \end{center} \\[0.15cm] The table shows summary statistics for Marcus's $12$ scores.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For Elena's scores, calculate

subparts.label: (i)

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: the median,

subparts.label: (iii)
subparts.prompt: the interquartile range.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the performances of Elena and Marcus using the median and the interquartile range.
markscheme: Marcus has a higher median ($8.5 > 8$), so on average Marcus scores higher than Elena [B1]
Elena has a smaller interquartile range ($2 < 3.5$), so Elena's scores are more consistent (less spread out) than Marcus's [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: In a competition, only scores of $10$ earn bonus points. The team coach states: "Because Marcus has both a higher mean and a higher median than Elena, Marcus must have scored more $10$s than Elena." Explain why the coach's statement is not necessarily true.
markscheme: Averages such as the mean and median do not show the individual frequencies of specific scores [B1]
Marcus could achieve a mean of $8.4$ and median of $8.5$ with fewer than two $10$s (for example, by scoring many $8$s and $9$s) [B1]

intro_text: Two battery manufacturers, Brand A and Brand B, test a sample of batteries to measure their battery life, in hours. The box-and-whisker plots show the distributions of battery life for Brand A and Brand B.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For Brand A, find

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: the median battery life,

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: the interquartile range.

parts.label: (b)

markscheme: Brand B has a higher median battery life ($27$ hours) than Brand A ($24$ hours), so on average Brand B batteries last longer [B1]
Brand A has a smaller interquartile range ($9$ hours) than Brand B ($12$ hours) (or smaller range: $22 < 27$), so Brand A's battery life is more consistent [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A reviewer claims: "The box-and-whisker plots show that the mean battery life of Brand B is greater than $27$ hours, and that more batteries were tested for Brand B than for Brand A."\\[0.15cm]Give two reasons why the reviewer's claim is not valid from the given diagram.
markscheme: Box-and-whisker plots show the median and quartiles, not the mean [B1]
Box-and-whisker plots do not show the sample size (number of batteries tested) for either brand [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: In a sample of $60$ Brand B batteries, estimate how many batteries lasted more than $21$ hours.
markscheme: $21$ hours is the lower quartile, so $\dfrac{3}{4} \times 60$ [M1]

intro_text: The back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the scores, out of $60$, achieved by $15$ students in Class A and $15$ students in Class B on a mathematics test.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: For Class A, find

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: the median,

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: the interquartile range.
markscheme: Identifies upper quartile $Q_3 = 42$ and lower quartile $Q_1 = 25$: $42 - 25$ [M1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For Class B, the median is $40$ and the interquartile range is $12$. \\[0.15cm] Compare the test scores of Class A and Class B.
markscheme: Compares averages: Class B achieved higher scores on average because its median ($40$) is higher than Class A's median ($34$) [B1]
Compares spread: Class B's scores are more consistent (less spread out) because its interquartile range ($12$) is smaller than Class A's interquartile range ($17$) [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A new student joins Class A and takes the test. The new median for the $16$ students in Class A is $34.5$. \\[0.15cm] Find the score of the new student.
markscheme: Identifies that the median of $16$ values is the mean of the $8$th and $9$th values: $\dfrac{34 + x}{2} = 34.5$ [M1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A teacher looks at the diagram and says, "More students scored above $45$ in Class B than in Class A, so Class B must have more students overall." \\[0.15cm] Explain why the teacher's reasoning is incorrect.
markscheme: Notes that both classes have the exact same total number of students ($15$ in each class) [B1]
Explains that having more scores above $45$ shows that Class B's scores are higher overall, not that the class has a larger total size [B1]

intro_text: Two machines, Machine $A$ and Machine $B$, fill packets of coffee. A random sample of $40$ packets from each machine is weighed. The table shows summary statistics for the masses, in grams, of the packets in each sample.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the total mass of the $40$ packets in the sample from Machine $A$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Make two statistical comparisons between the masses of the packets filled by Machine $A$ and Machine $B$.
markscheme: Average comparison: On average, Machine $B$ fills heavier packets because its median is higher ($251.0\text{ g} > 250.2\text{ g}$) (or Machine $A$ has a higher mean mass, $250.4\text{ g} > 249.8\text{ g}$) [B2] (or valid statement without quoting values [B1])

Spread comparison: Machine $A$ fills packets with more consistent masses because its interquartile range ($1.8\text{ g} < 3.4\text{ g}$) and range ($5.6\text{ g} < 11.2\text{ g}$) are smaller [B2] (or valid statement without quoting values [B1])

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why the median and interquartile range are more appropriate measures than the mean and range for comparing these two samples.
markscheme: Machine $B$ has a very large range ($11.2\text{ g}$) relative to its IQR ($3.4\text{ g}$) and its mean is lower than its median, indicating extreme low values (outliers) [B1]
The median and interquartile range are not distorted by extreme values / outliers [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A supervisor claims that Machine $B$ must have produced at least one packet weighing less than $242$ g. Explain whether the supervisor's claim must be true.
markscheme: No, the claim does not have to be true because the minimum and maximum values are unknown [B1]
For example, the masses in Machine $B$ could range from $243.0$ g to $254.2$ g (giving a range of $11.2$ g and median $251.0$ g) with no packet below $242$ g [B1]

intro_text: The back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the test scores, out of $60$, of $15$ students in Class A and $15$ students in Class B.

markscheme: On average, Class B scored higher than Class A because the median for Class B ($44$) is greater than the median for Class A ($38$) [B1]
The scores in Class B are more consistent (less spread out) than in Class A because the interquartile range for Class B ($13$) is smaller than for Class A ($16$) [B1]

markscheme: The distributions of scores overlap, so some individual scores in Class A are higher than some scores in Class B [B1]
For example, the highest score in Class A is $54$, which is higher than the lowest score in Class B of $28$ [B1]

parts.prompt: Another class, Class C, has $30$ students and a mean test score of $41$. Calculate the combined mean test score of all $60$ students in Class A, Class B, and Class C.
markscheme: Total score for Class A $= 580$ and total score for Class B $= 650$ [M1]

intro_text: A technology company tests a new operating system on two smartphone models, Model A and Model B. The table shows the results of Test 2, carried out after the system update.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the overall mean battery drain for all $80$ devices tested in Test 2.

parts.label: (b)

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Show that the overall mean battery drain in Test 1 was $16.50\%$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: The company's marketing team claims: "Because the overall mean battery drain fell from $16.50\%$ to $16.15\%$, the update improved battery efficiency." Explain why this conclusion is misleading, referring to the data for both models.
markscheme: The mean battery drain actually worsened (increased) for both models individually: Model A rose from $17.5\%$ to $18.4\%$ and Model B rose from $13.5\%$ to $14.8\%$ [B1]
The overall mean only decreased because Test 2 included a much higher proportion of Model B devices ($50$ instead of $20$), which have a lower baseline drain [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: In Test 2, the minimum battery drain recorded for Model A was $15.1\%$ and the minimum battery drain recorded for Model B was $9.2\%$.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Write down the maximum battery drain recorded for Model A.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the overall range of battery drain for all $80$ devices combined in Test 2.
markscheme: Maximum for Model B $= 9.2 + 11.5 = 20.7\%$, so overall maximum $= 21.3\%$ and overall minimum $= 9.2\%$ [M1]

intro_text: A nutritionist investigates the sugar content, $s$ grams, in $60$ breakfast cereals from Brand $X$ and $50$ breakfast cereals from Brand $Y$. parts.prompt: The estimated mean sugar content of the $50$ Brand $Y$ cereals is $18.6$ grams. Calculate the values of $a$ and $b$.

The sugar content of Brand $Y$ cereals is more consistent because Brand $Y$ has a smaller interquartile range ($13.5 < 16$) [B1]

intro_text: A research institute investigates the daily screen time, in minutes, of two groups of users: Group P (teenagers) and Group Q (adults). The table shows summary statistics for the two groups.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: When Group P and Group Q are combined into a single group of $(80 + n)$ users, the overall mean daily screen time is $185$ minutes.\\[0.15cm]Calculate the value of $n$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the daily screen time of Group P and Group Q using the median and the interquartile range.
markscheme: Group P has a higher median screen time ($210$ minutes) than Group Q ($160$ minutes), so on average Group P spends more time on screens [B1]
Group P has a smaller interquartile range ($70$ minutes) than Group Q ($80$ minutes), so Group P's screen times are less spread out / more consistent [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A journalist reads the table and concludes: "Because the mean daily screen time for Group P is $215$ minutes and for Group Q is $165$ minutes, every teenager in Group P spent more time on screens than the average adult in Group Q."\\[0.15cm]Explain why this conclusion is incorrect, and state one limitation of using only this table to compare all teenagers and adults.
markscheme: The mean is only an average; Group P's lower quartile is $175$ minutes, so at least $25\%$ of Group P users spent $175$ minutes or less (and some could spend less than $165$ minutes) [B1]
The table does not show extreme values (minimum/maximum) or how the samples were chosen, so results may not represent the wider populations [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: In a follow-up survey, $40$ additional adults are added to Group Q. Every one of these $40$ adults has a daily screen time of $100$ minutes.\\[0.15cm]State the new value of the lower quartile of Group Q, explaining your answer.
markscheme: Group Q now has $120 + 40 = 160$ users, so the lower quartile is at the $40$th ordered value ($25\%$ of $160 = 40$) [M1]
Since all $40$ new adults have a screen time of $100$ minutes (which is less than the previous lower quartile of $125$ minutes), at least the lowest $40$ values are now $100$ minutes [A1]

intro_text: Two classes, Class A and Class B, take the same mathematics examination.\n- Class A has $25$ students. Their mean score is $68.4$ and their range is $34$.\n- Class B has $30$ students. Their scores, $s$, are summarised in the grouped frequency table below.

parts.label: (a)

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the combined mean score of all $55$ students in Class A and Class B.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The headteacher concludes that Class A performed better overall than Class B because Class A has a higher mean score. Give two reasons why the headteacher's conclusion should be treated with caution.
markscheme: Class B's mean ($67.7$) is only an estimate from grouped data, so its true mean could actually be higher than Class A's mean ($68.4$) [B1]
Comparing only the mean ignores the spread of scores or possible outliers in the two classes [B1]

intro_text: The two pie charts show the distribution of customer complaints received by Store P and Store Q across four categories: Delivery, Quality, Pricing, and Service.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the value of $x$ in the pie chart for Store P.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A manager looks at the two pie charts and claims that Store P received more complaints about Delivery than Store Q because the sector angle for Delivery is larger in Store P ($126^\circ > 108^\circ$). Explain why the manager's claim may be incorrect.
markscheme: Pie charts only show proportions (or percentages) and not the total number of complaints at each store [B1]
If Store Q received a larger total number of complaints than Store P, Store Q could have more Delivery complaints [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Store P received $140$ complaints about Delivery. Calculate the total number of complaints received by Store P.

parts.prompt: In the following month, Store P reduces its Delivery complaints by $20\%$ and its Pricing complaints by $15\%$, while the number of Quality and Service complaints remains unchanged. Calculate the new sector angle for Delivery when a new pie chart is drawn for Store P.
markscheme: Original Pricing complaints $= \dfrac{72}{360} \times 400 = 80$, so new Pricing complaints $= 80 \times 0.85 = 68$ [M1]

intro_text: Two courier companies, Company A and Company B, each record the delivery times, $t$ minutes, for $100$ parcels. The grouped frequency table shows the distribution of delivery times for Company A, where $x$ and $y$ are positive integers.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For Company A, an estimate of the mean delivery time, calculated using the midpoints of the intervals, is $24.6$ minutes.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Show that $3x + 7y = 216$.
markscheme: $15x + 35y = 1080$ dividing by $5$ to give $3x + 7y = 216$ with no errors seen [A1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Use the total number of parcels to form a second equation in $x$ and $y$, and solve the two simultaneous equations to find the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For Company B, the $100$ delivery times have a mean of $26.2$ minutes, a median of $22.0$ minutes and an interquartile range of $18.5$ minutes. Write down the class interval that contains the median delivery time for Company A, and compare the mean delivery times of the two companies.
markscheme: Cumulative frequencies $14$, $30$, $68$ identified so $50\text{th}$ and $51\text{st}$ values lie in $20 < t \le 30$ [M1]
Company A has a lower mean delivery time ($24.6 < 26.2$), so on average Company A delivers parcels faster than Company B [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A customer claims: "At least $45\%$ of Company A's parcels were delivered in $25$ minutes or less." State the minimum and maximum possible percentages of Company A's parcels delivered in $25$ minutes or less, and explain why the customer's claim cannot be confirmed.
markscheme: The data is grouped, so the exact delivery times of the $38$ parcels in $20 < t \le 30$ are unknown and the true percentage could be as low as $30\%$ [B1]

intro_text: Company A employs $80$ workers. The table shows the distribution of their annual salaries, $\$s$ thousand.

Compares IQRs: Branch South's overtime hours are much more consistent (less spread out) because its interquartile range ($3.4$ hours) is smaller than Branch North's ($5.8$ hours) [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Using the true continuous class intervals from part (a), calculate an estimate of the mean delay time of the $60$ trains. Give your answer as a mixed number or correct to $3$ significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: For the $60$ trains, the total number of passengers is $7440$. Two additional delayed trains are then included in the study, so that the exact mean number of passengers across all $62$ trains is $125$.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the total number of passengers on the two additional trains.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: One of the two additional trains carried $k$ passengers and the other carried $(2k - 14)$ passengers. Find the number of passengers on each of the two additional trains, and explain how the discrete nature of $p$ confirms that your answers are valid.
markscheme: Since $p$ is discrete data, the number of passengers must be a positive whole number, which both $108$ and $202$ satisfy [B1]

intro_text: Do not use a calculator in this question.\\[0.15cm]A botanist investigates $100$ plants in a greenhouse. The stem length, $L$ cm, of each plant is continuous data, recorded to the nearest centimetre in the table.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Explain why there appears to be a gap between $14$ cm and $15$ cm in the table even though stem length is continuous data.
markscheme: The lengths were rounded to the nearest centimetre, so values between $14.5$ cm and $15$ cm are rounded up into $15 - 19$ and values below $14.5$ cm are rounded down into $10 - 14$ [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Write down the true continuous class interval for the group recorded as $15 - 19$ cm, giving your answer in the form $a \le L < b$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A histogram is drawn to represent the continuous stem length distribution.\\[0.15cm]On the histogram, the bar representing the recorded group $15 - 19$ cm has width $2$ cm and height $10$ cm.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the width and the height of the bar representing the recorded group $20 - 29$ cm.
markscheme: True class width $= 29.5 - 19.5 = 10$ cm (twice $5$ cm), so bar width $= 4$ cm [B1]
Frequency density $= \dfrac{40}{10} = 4$ (compared to $\dfrac{25}{5} = 5$), so bar height $= \dfrac{4}{5} \times 10 = 8$ cm [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the height of the bar representing the recorded group $30 - 44$ cm, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
markscheme: True class width $= 44.5 - 29.5 = 15$ cm, so frequency density $= \dfrac{20}{15} = \dfrac{4}{3}$ [M1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For the same $100$ plants, the number of leaves on each plant is discrete data.\\[0.15cm]- $k$ plants have $4$ leaves.\\[0.15cm]- $(2k + 3)$ plants have $5$ leaves.\\[0.15cm]- $(3k - 1)$ plants have $6$ leaves.\\[0.15cm]- $2k$ plants have $7$ leaves.\\[0.15cm]- $18$ plants have $8$ leaves.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Show that $k = 10$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Find the median number of leaves and calculate the exact mean number of leaves per plant.
markscheme: Frequencies are $10, 23, 29, 20, 18$; $50$th and $51$st values give Median $= 6$ [B1]

intro_text: In an experiment, two variables $X$ and $Y$ are recorded for a set of $n$ trials, where $n$ is a positive integer:\n- $X$ is a discrete variable that can only take integer values such that $2 < X \le 6$.\n- $Y$ is a continuous variable that can take any real value such that $2 < Y \le 6$.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: List all possible values of $X$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Explain why it is impossible to list all possible values of $Y$.
markscheme: $Y$ is continuous, so between any two values of $Y$ there are infinitely many other real values [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: In $n$ trials, the discrete variable $X$ takes the value $3$ on $k$ trials, the value $4$ on $(2k + 2)$ trials, the value $5$ on $(k + 3)$ trials, and the value $6$ on $3$ trials.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Find an expression, in terms of $k$, for the total number of trials, $n$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Given that the mean value of $X$ across all $n$ trials is $4.45$, calculate the value of $k$ and hence state the value of $n$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: In the same $20$ trials, the continuous variable $Y$ is grouped into two intervals: $2 < Y \le 4$ with frequency $11$, and $4 < Y \le 6$ with frequency $9$.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate for the mean value of $Y$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Explain why the mean of $X$ in part (b)(ii) is exact, whereas the mean of $Y$ in part (c)(i) is only an estimate.
markscheme: $X$ is discrete so every individual trial takes one of the exact known integer values $3, 4, 5$ or $6$ [B1]
$Y$ is continuous and grouped into intervals, so the exact individual values are unknown and midpoints must be used [B1]

intro_text:
Do not use a calculator in this question. An environmental scientist records two sets of data at a monitoring station over a $60$-day period:
- Set $A$: The number of fish caught in a net each day (discrete data).
- Set $B$: The daily rainfall, $r$ mm (continuous data).
The results are summarised in the two tables below.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The exact mean number of fish caught per day in Set $A$ is $1.4$. Find the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate an estimate for the mean daily rainfall in Set $B$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why the mean calculated in part (a) is an exact value, whereas the mean calculated in part (b) is only an estimate.
markscheme: Set $A$ is discrete data where the exact frequency of every individual integer outcome ($0, 1, 2, 3$) is known [B1]
Set $B$ is continuous data grouped into class intervals, so individual daily measurements are unknown and class midpoints must be used [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find the number of days on which the daily rainfall was at least $10$ mm, and state whether this value is exact or an estimate.
markscheme: Value is Exact (since $10$ is an exact class boundary between $5 \le r < 10$ and $10 \le r < 20$) [B1]

intro_text: A quality-control engineer inspects batches of precision steel rods. Two variables are recorded: $d$, the number of defective rods in a batch, and $L$, the length of a rod in millimetres. In a sample of $40$ batches, the distribution of $d$ is shown in the table below, where $x$ and $y$ are positive integers. The mean number of defective rods per batch is $1.25$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Form two simultaneous equations in $x$ and $y$, and solve them to find the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the median and the interquartile range of $d$, the number of defective rods per batch.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A trainee records the lengths, $L$ mm, of a sample of rods using the intervals $50$ to $54$, $55$ to $59$, and $60$ to $64$. Explain why this notation is suitable for discrete data such as $d$, but unsuitable for continuous data such as $L$.
markscheme: For discrete data, values only take integers so no values exist between $54$ and $55$ [B1]
For continuous data, measurements can take decimal values between $54$ and $55$ (such as $54.3$ mm), leaving gaps unless written as continuous inequalities [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The lengths, $L$ mm, of $60$ rods are correctly grouped into continuous intervals: $18$ rods have $49.5 \le L < 54.5$, $30$ rods have $54.5 \le L < 59.5$, and $12$ rods have $59.5 \le L < 64.5$. Calculate the greatest possible value of the mean length of the $60$ rods.

intro_text: A weather station records four different types of data each month.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Complete the table by writing Discrete or Continuous in each row.
markscheme: At least two rows correct from Discrete, Continuous, Continuous, Discrete [B1]
All four rows correct: Discrete, Continuous, Continuous, Discrete [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Daily rainfall, $r$ mm, is grouped into class intervals. \\[0.15cm] Explain why the intervals should be written as $0 \le r < 5$ and $5 \le r < 10$ rather than $0 - 4$ and $5 - 9$.
markscheme: Rainfall is continuous data, so values between $4$ and $5$ (such as $4.3$ mm) can occur [B1]
Writing $0 - 4$ and $5 - 9$ leaves a gap where values cannot be placed [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The number of days with rain in a month is recorded as $12$, which is an integer. \\[0.15cm] Explain why this data is discrete even though time itself is continuous.
markscheme: We are counting the number of separate days, which can only be whole numbers [B1]

intro_text: A transport researcher collects data at an airport:\n- Table $1$ shows the number of suitcases, $n$, carried by each of $50$ passengers.\n- Table $2$ shows the mass, $m$ kilograms, of $50$ suitcases weighed at check-in.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the data in Table $1$ is discrete while the data in Table $2$ is continuous.
markscheme: The number of suitcases is counted and takes only integer values, whereas mass is measured and can take any value within a continuous interval [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Write down the upper bound for the mass of a suitcase in the interval $30 < m \le 40$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of the $50$ suitcases in Table $2$.

intro_text: A maternity clinic records four pieces of information for each newborn baby: length ($l$ cm), mass ($m$ g), number of older siblings ($s$), and heart rate ($r$ beats per minute).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write down the two variables that represent continuous data.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The length of one baby is measured as $50.4$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place. Write down the lower bound and the upper bound for the actual length $l$ of this baby.
parts.answer_format: Lower bound = ..... cm , upper bound = ..... cm

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A student draws a bar chart with gaps between the bars for the number of older siblings ($s$), and a histogram with no gaps between the bars for the masses ($m$). Explain why this choice of statistical diagrams is appropriate.
markscheme: Number of older siblings is discrete data, so gaps between bars show separate, isolated integer values [B1]
Mass is continuous data, so no gaps between bars show a continuous scale with no breaks between intervals [B1]

intro_text:
A garden centre records two different measurements for $50$ potted plants:
- The number of flowers, $n$, on each plant.
- The height, $h$\,cm, of each plant.

The two frequency tables show the results.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State which variable, $n$ or $h$, is continuous data, and give a reason for your answer.
markscheme: Height is measured rather than counted and can take any value within a range [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the intervals for $h$ are written using inequality signs such as $10 < h \le 15$, whereas the values of $n$ are written as single integers.
markscheme: $n$ is discrete data so it only takes exact integer values [B1]
$h$ is continuous data so inequality intervals are needed to include all possible measured values without gaps [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the exact mean number of flowers per plant.

intro_text: An athletics coach records two variables for each of $40$ runners at a training session:\n- Variable $X$: The number of laps completed by each runner.\n- Variable $Y$: The time, $t$ minutes, taken by each runner to complete $5$ km.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State which variable is discrete and which variable is continuous.

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: The results for Variable $Y$ are grouped in the frequency table below.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Explain why the class intervals are written using inequality signs such as $18 < t \le 20$ instead of whole-number ranges such as $18 - 20$.
markscheme: Time is continuous data, so non-integer values between $20$ and $21$ (such as $20.4$) would otherwise be excluded [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate for the mean time taken by the $40$ runners.

intro_text: A biologist conducts an experiment on $40$ seedlings. \\[0.15cm] For each seedling, the biologist records:\n- $L$: the stem length, in centimetres, measured to the nearest $0.1$ cm,\n- $N$: the number of leaves on the stem.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: One seedling has a recorded stem length of $L = 12.4$ cm and $N = 6$ leaves.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: State whether $L$ is discrete or continuous data.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Write down the lower bound and the upper bound for the actual stem length of this seedling.
subparts.answer_format: Lower bound = ..... cm , Upper bound = ..... cm

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: The stem lengths, $L$ cm, of all $40$ seedlings are shown in the cumulative frequency diagram.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Use the cumulative frequency diagram to estimate the number of seedlings with a stem length greater than $10$ cm.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Explain why a continuous curve is drawn to join the points on this cumulative frequency diagram.
markscheme: Stem length is continuous data, so all intermediate values between the plotted points can occur [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The biologist also records the number of leaves, $N$, for each of the $40$ seedlings and finds that the mean is $5.35$ leaves. \\[0.15cm] Explain why $N$ is still classified as discrete data even though its mean is a decimal.
markscheme: Each individual seedling has a whole number of leaves (counted data) [B1]
Calculating the mean divides the total by $40$, which can produce a non-integer average even for discrete data [B1]

intro_text: A botanical garden measures the heights, $h$ cm, of $50$ young plants. Each height is measured correct to the nearest centimetre and grouped into the table below.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the heights of the plants are continuous data, even though every recorded value in the table is a whole number.
markscheme: Height is a continuous measurement that can take any value, and it has only been rounded to the nearest whole centimetre [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Write down the lower bound and the upper bound for the true height, $h$ cm, of a plant in the $15 - 19$ group.
parts.answer_format: Lower bound = ..... cm , Upper bound = ..... cm

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate an estimate for the mean height of the $50$ plants.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A student states that none of the $50$ plants had a true height of $14.7$ cm because $14.7$ does not appear in either $10 - 14$ or $15 - 19$. Explain why the student is incorrect.
markscheme: Height is continuous, so a plant with a true height of $14.7$ cm rounds to $15$ cm to the nearest centimetre [B1]
Therefore, it is included in the $15 - 19$ class interval [B1]

intro_text: A quality-control engineer inspects a random sample of $50$ machined metal bolts.\nThe table shows the number of surface defects ($d$) found on each bolt.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the mean number of surface defects per bolt.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Explain why the mean number of surface defects can be a non-integer value for other samples even though $d$ is discrete data.
markscheme: The mean is a calculated numerical average across all bolts in the sample rather than a count of defects on a single bolt [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: The masses, $m$ grams, of the same $50$ bolts are measured as continuous data and grouped into the frequency table below.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of a bolt.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: A bolt is rejected if its mass is $51.0$ g or more, or if it has more than $2$ surface defects.\nState the maximum possible number of bolts that could be rejected from this sample of $50$ bolts, explaining your reasoning.
markscheme: There are $9$ bolts with $m \ge 51.0$ g and $4 + 2 = 6$ bolts with $d > 2$; the maximum total occurs if none of these bolts overlap ($9 + 6 = 15$) [B1]

intro_text: A courier company records two variables for each of $60$ deliveries made in one week:\\[0.15cm]- the number of parcels, $n$, in each delivery (Table 1),\\[0.15cm]- the total mass, $m$ kg, of each delivery (Table 2).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why continuous inequality intervals such as $0 < m \le 5$ are used in Table 2, whereas single integers are used in Table 1.
markscheme: Mass is continuous data and can take any decimal value between boundaries, so inequality intervals prevent gaps or overlaps [B1]
Number of parcels is discrete data and can only take exact whole-number values [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean number of parcels per delivery, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of a delivery.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why the mean calculated in part (c) is only an estimate, whereas the mean calculated in part (b) is exact.
markscheme: In Table 2 the continuous data is grouped so individual masses are unknown and mid-interval values are used as approximations, whereas in Table 1 every exact discrete value is known [B1]

intro_text: A botanist studies $50$ plants in a greenhouse. For each plant, she records $n$, the number of leaves, and $h$, the height in centimetres. The results are shown in the two tables.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the mean number of leaves calculated from the first table is an exact value, whereas the mean height calculated from the second table is only an estimate.
markscheme: The number of leaves ($n$) is discrete data, so the exact integer value for every plant is known from the table [B1]
Height ($h$) is continuous data grouped into class intervals, so individual plant heights are unknown and mid-interval values must be used [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: Calculate

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: the exact mean number of leaves per plant,

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: an estimate of the mean height of the $50$ plants.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the greatest possible range of the heights of the $50$ plants.

intro_text: A marine biologist studies a sample of $50$ adult sea turtles. For each turtle, the biologist records $n$, the number of barnacles attached to its shell, and $m$, the mass of the turtle in kilograms, measured to the nearest $0.1$ kg. The masses of the $50$ turtles are summarised in the table below.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State which variable, $n$ or $m$, is discrete data and which variable is continuous data, giving a reason for each choice.
markscheme: $n$ is discrete because the number of barnacles is counted and can only take whole number values [B1]
$m$ is continuous because mass is measured and can take any value within a continuous range [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use the table of masses to answer the following.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Explain why the masses are grouped into class intervals using inequalities such as $30.0 \le m < 35.0$ rather than listing individual values.
markscheme: Continuous measurements can take any decimal value in a range (so individual values rarely repeat) and inequalities group all possible values without gaps or overlaps [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of the $50$ turtles.
markscheme: Mid-interval values $32.5$, $37.5$, $42.5$, and $47.5$ seen or used [M1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Because each mass $m$ was measured to the nearest $0.1$ kg, a turtle recorded as having a mass of $35.0$ kg actually has a true mass $w$ kg in the interval $a \le w < b$. Write down the values of $a$ and $b$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The discrete variable $n$ has a mean of $14.6$ barnacles for the $50$ turtles. Explain why the mean of a discrete variable can be a decimal number even though the data values themselves can only be integers.
markscheme: The mean is calculated by dividing the total number of barnacles ($730$) by $50$, which does not have to result in a whole number [B1]

intro_text: A marine biologist studies a sample of $60$ fish in a lake. Two measurements are recorded for each fish: the number of parasites on the fish, and the length, $L$ cm, of the fish.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State which of the two measurements is continuous data, and explain why continuous data is usually grouped using inequalities such as $10 < L \le 15$ rather than listed as individual values.
markscheme: Continuous data can take infinitely many possible decimal/fractional values within an interval, so individual values rarely repeat and inequalities ensure every possible measurement is included without gaps [B1]

parts.label: (b)

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Find the value of $k$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate for the mean length of the $60$ fish.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A student states: "Exactly $35$ of the $60$ fish have a length of $22$ cm or less." Explain why this statement cannot be confirmed from the table.
markscheme: Because length is continuous and grouped in $20 < L \le 25$, the exact lengths of those $20$ fish are unknown (so the true number could be anywhere from $25$ to $45$) [A1]

intro_text: A botanist records the number of leaves, $n$, on each of $40$ plants in a greenhouse. \\[0.15cm] The frequency table shows the results.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: State whether the number of leaves, $n$, is discrete or continuous data, and give a reason for your answer.
markscheme: Discrete, because the number of leaves is counted and can only take whole-number (integer) values [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the mean number of leaves per plant.

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: The botanist also measures the height, $h$ cm, of the same $40$ plants.
parts.prompt: The grouped frequency table below shows the heights of the $40$ plants.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: State whether the height, $h$ cm, is discrete or continuous data, and give a reason for your answer.
markscheme: Continuous, because height is measured on a continuous scale and can take any value within a range [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean height of the $40$ plants.

subparts.label: (iii)
subparts.prompt: Explain why the mean calculated in part (b)(ii) is only an estimate, whereas the mean calculated in part (a)(ii) is an exact value.
markscheme: In part (b)(ii), the continuous heights are grouped into intervals so individual plant heights are unknown and mid-interval values must be used [B1]
In part (a)(ii), every discrete value of $n$ is known exactly from the ungrouped frequency table [B1]

intro_text: A bakery produces boxes of biscuits. For each box, two quantities are checked:\n- $N$, the number of broken biscuits in the box.\n- $M$, the total mass of the biscuits in the box, in grams.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State which of $N$ and $M$ is discrete and which is continuous.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: In a sample of $40$ boxes, the distribution of $N$ is shown in the bar chart. Calculate the percentage of boxes in the sample that contain fewer than $2$ broken biscuits.

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: The mass, $M$, of one box of biscuits is recorded as $450$\,g, correct to the nearest $5$\,g.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Write down the lower bound and the upper bound of $M$.
subparts.answer_format: Lower bound = ..... g , Upper bound = ..... g

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Explain why $N$ cannot have a lower bound of $1.5$ when recorded as $2$ broken biscuits, whereas $M$ can have non-integer bounds.
markscheme: $N$ is discrete data so it only takes exact integer values and is not rounded [B1]
$M$ is continuous data so any recorded value represents an interval of possible actual measurements [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A box is rejected if $N > 2$ or if $M < 448$\,g. State, with a reason, whether a box with $N = 2$ and $M = 450$\,g (correct to the nearest $5$\,g) could be rejected.
markscheme: Because $M$ is continuous, its actual mass could lie in the interval $447.5 \le M < 448$, even though $N = 2$ is exact [B1]

intro_text: A warehouse records the number of items inside each of $50$ parcels and also measures the mass, $m$ kilograms, of each parcel. The grouped frequency table summarises the masses of the $50$ parcels.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the mass of a parcel is continuous data, whereas the number of items inside the parcel is discrete data.
markscheme: Mass is measured and can take any value on a continuous scale (e.g. $2.35$ kg) [B1]
The number of items is counted and can only take whole-number values [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The mass of one parcel is recorded as $4.6$ kg, correct to $1$ decimal place. Write down the lower bound and the upper bound of the actual mass of this parcel.
parts.answer_format: Lower bound = ..... kg , Upper bound = ..... kg

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The number of items inside another parcel is $n$, where $12 < n \le 15$. Write down all the possible values of $n$.
markscheme: $13, 14, 15$ [B2] (or any two correct with no extras [B1])

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of the $50$ parcels.

intro_text: An agricultural scientist investigates two variables for $80$ apple trees in an orchard:\n- Table $1$ shows the number of apples, $N$, harvested from each tree, where $p$ and $q$ are positive integers.\n- Table $2$ shows the total mass of apples, $M$ kilograms, harvested from each tree.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why Table $1$ uses intervals such as $20 \le N \le 29$ and $30 \le N \le 39$ with a numerical gap between $29$ and $30$, whereas Table $2$ uses intervals such as $4 < M \le 6$ and $6 < M \le 8$ with no gap.
markscheme: The number of apples ($N$) is discrete data, so no values can occur between $29$ and $30$ [B1]
Mass ($M$) is continuous data, so values can lie anywhere on a continuous scale and require contiguous intervals with no gaps [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The estimated mean number of apples per tree, calculated using the mid-interval values of Table $1$, is $39.25$. Calculate the values of $p$ and $q$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use Table $2$ and the estimated mean number of apples per tree.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of apples harvested per tree.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Hence calculate an estimate of the mean mass of a single apple in the orchard. Give your answer in grams, correct to $3$ significant figures.

intro_text: A logistics company analyses the daily deliveries made by its drivers. Two variables are recorded for a sample of $50$ drivers on a Monday: \\[0.15cm] $\bullet$ $x$, the number of parcels delivered by a driver \\[0.15cm] $\bullet$ $d$ km, the total distance driven by a driver

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Classify each of the variables $x$ and $d$ as either discrete or continuous data, giving a brief reason for each classification.
markscheme: $x$ is discrete because the number of parcels is counted and can only take integer values [B1]
$d$ is continuous because distance is measured and can take any real value within a range [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: For the discrete variable $x$, the number of parcels delivered by the $50$ drivers is summarised in the frequency table below, where $p$ and $q$ are positive integers.

markscheme: As the distance from the city centre increases, the monthly rent decreases [B1]

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Show that $p + q = 21$.
markscheme: Sum of $x$-values for the $9$ plotted apartments $= 58$ and sum of $y$-values $= 121$ [B1]

parts.context: The remaining two cars have ages $a$ years and $b$ years, with resale values $13.8$ thousand dollars and $8.6$ thousand dollars respectively. The equation of the line of regression of $y$ on $x$ for all $9$ cars is $y = -1.8x + 26.4$.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate $\bar{y}$, the mean resale value in thousand dollars of all $9$ cars.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Use the regression equation to show that $a + b = 17$.
markscheme: $\dfrac{37 + a + b}{9} = 6$, leading to $a + b = 17$ with no errors seen [A1]

subparts.label: (iii)
subparts.prompt: Given that the older of these two cars is $3$ years older than the younger car, find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$, where $a < b$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Interpret the value $-1.8$ in the regression equation $y = -1.8x + 26.4$ in the context of this question.
markscheme: The resale value decreases by $1.8$ thousand dollars (or $1800$ dollars) for each additional year of age [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the difference between the actual resale value of the $4$-year-old car and the resale value predicted by the regression equation.

intro_text: A marine biologist investigates the relationship between water depth, $d$ metres, and water temperature, $T$ $^\circ$C, at $8$ locations in a lake. The table shows the recorded measurements.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Use your graphic display calculator to find the equation of the linear regression line in the form $T = md + c$, giving the values of $m$ and $c$ correct to $3$ significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Interpret the value of $m$ and the value of $c$ in the context of this investigation.
markscheme: $m$: For each additional $1$ metre of depth, the water temperature decreases on average by $0.418$ $^\circ$C [B1]
$c$: The estimated water temperature at the surface ($d = 0$ m) is $23.1$ $^\circ$C [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: A ninth measurement is taken at a depth of $k$ metres, where the recorded temperature is $12.2$ $^\circ$C. When all $9$ measurements are included, the new mean depth is $19$ metres.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Find the value of $k$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Determine whether the ninth point $(k, 12.2)$ lies above or below the original regression line found in part (a), showing your working clearly.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The marine biologist uses the regression equation to estimate the water temperature at a depth of $65$ metres and obtains a negative temperature. Give two reasons why this estimate is not valid.
markscheme: $65$ metres is well outside the range of observed depths ($4$ m to $32$ m), so extrapolation is unreliable [B1]
In a lake, water temperature cannot drop below $0$ $^\circ$C without freezing (the linear trend does not continue at greater depths) [B1]

intro_text: A technology company records the age, $x$ months, and the resale value, $\$y$, of $8$ identical laptops. The scatter diagram shows the $8$ data points and the regression line of $y$ on $x$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ of the $8$ laptops.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y = ax + b$. Given that the regression line intersects the $y$-axis at $(0, 1200)$, find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$.
markscheme: Using the property that the regression line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = (18, 660)$: $660 = 18a + 1200$ [M1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: A $9$th laptop is added to the data set. Its age is $x_9$ months and its resale value is $\$y_9$. When all $9$ laptops are included, the new mean age is $19$ months and the new mean resale value is $\$640$.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the value of $x_9$ and the value of $y_9$.
markscheme: Total age for $9$ laptops $= 9 \times 19 = 171$ and total resale value $= 9 \times 640 = 5760$ [M1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Determine whether the point $(x_9, y_9)$ lies above, below, or on the original regression line. Show working to support your answer.

parts.label: (b)

parts.label: (d)

subparts.label: (i)

parts.label: (c)
